en: *Anusāralakṣaṇa-śāstra*, one fascicle,
composed by Dharma Master Guṇamati;
translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India during the Chen dynasty.
In the treatise, the sixteen truths (*ṣoḍaśatattva*) are explained. A general question regarding these sixteen truths is posed:
"Are there sixteen entities, or are there sixteen names?
The answer is:

The term *vipaśyanā* (毘防夷反頗判何反沙) is translated as "extensive understanding" (*guǎngjiě*). According to the Master’s interpretation, there are sixteen objects (*vastu*) for this [insight], and thus sixteen names are established; because these actually possess substantial entities (*dravya*), they are called "objects."

The *Upadeśa* (Exegesis) is translated as "the Teacher’s Explanation of the Cultivation of Goodness for the Sake of Detachment from Desire. There are sixteen names [for these exegeses], yet there are only seven entities, and four [categories] within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
That is to say, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; with one each for the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, these together constitute seven.

The Buddha originally taught the *Upadeśa* sūtras to explain various meanings. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda, Kātyāyana, and others recited what they had previously heard to explain the meanings within the sūtras. Because these works were like treatises composed by disciples to explain the sūtras, they are called *Sūtra-upadeśa*.
Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* emerged from the *Upadeśa*, being an abridgment of the *Upadeśa*;
since it was transmitted as an oral tradition, it is not called the "Sūtra-Vibhāṣā."
For now, we shall first rely on the previous explanation.
It is called "impermanent" because it is dependent upon conditions; conditioned phenomena lack inherent power and cannot arise by themselves, arising only by relying on conditions.
This is like an infant who cannot stand up by himself, but must rely on the support of others to rise again.
What is called "condition" refers to craving and karma.
It is only when these two factors are fully present that the five aggregates can arise.
Karma is capable of producing a fruit; yet even though it is capable of production, if there is no craving and attachment for a place of rebirth, the fruit will not arise.
Just as earth, water, and so forth can produce a grain sprout, yet if human effort is absent and the grain seed is not placed in the ground, the sprout will ultimately never arise;
likewise, when craving and karma have not yet arisen, the fruit does not arise.
Through the conjunction of craving and the causal conditions of karma, the fruit is then produced; once produced, it exists.
If the power of karma is exhausted, the fruit then passes away and ceases, returning once more to non-existence.
This refers to priority and posteriority; priority and posteriority have no inherent connection because they depend upon conditions.
It is said that because they depend upon conditions, they are impermanent.
Because their nature is one of oppression and affliction, they are suffering.
There are two kinds of affliction: first, affliction through opposition; second, affliction through compliance.
Regarding the disciples of the Buddha, this refers to affliction through opposition.
The disciples of the Buddha constantly give rise to fear within the cycle of birth and death; as a sutra illustrates:

"It is like a sharp sword being heated until its fiery light dazzles the eyes; if a person holds it at their side with the intent to harm them, they will constantly give rise to great terror in every thought-moment."
The disciples of the Buddha fear birth and death in this same way.
From here on follows the meaning of opposition:
because birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth constantly oppress and afflict them, they are suffering.
If it conforms to and afflicts ordinary beings—
since ordinary beings are attached to birth and death, this is the meaning of "conforming"—
it is like two brothers: though the elder brother deeply loves his younger brother and the younger brother constantly torments him, the elder brother still loves him despite enduring that torment.
Ordinary beings are attached to birth and death; even while undergoing suffering, they still cling to it. Therefore, its nature of oppression and affliction is defined as suffering (*duḥkha*).
It is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) because it serves as the antidote to the view of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*).
Ordinary beings cling to all phenomena, asserting them to be "mine"; now it is clarified that none of them are mine. It is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā) as an antidote to this view.
It is called "non-self" because it serves as the antidote to the view of self.

Ordinary beings grasp at the five aggregates and so forth as being a self; now, it is clarified that all phenomena are entirely devoid of self. To counteract this view, "non-self" is taught. These four constitute the Truth of Suffering.
Next, the four names of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) are explained.
Because it is the principle of the nature of seeds, it is called the "cause" (*hetu*), as it is capable of producing a fruit.
That this nature of seeds possesses four meanings constitutes its underlying principle.

Regarding the four meanings: first, if the seed is broken, it can no longer produce [a sprout]; for example, if one takes a seed and grinds it until it is broken, even if all other conditions are present, it will no longer be able to produce a shoot.
Afflictions such as craving are also seeds that produce fruits; if they are destroyed by the Path, even though other conditions are present, they can no longer produce fruit.
Second, because the seeds are old and decayed, even when all conditions are present, they cannot produce sprouts, as the seeds have endured for a long period of time.

The production of fruits by craving and so forth is likewise the case: Śrāvakas practice for sixty great eons, Pratyekabuddhas practice for one hundred great eons, and Buddhas practice for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

Before those of the three vehicles have yet resolved their minds, while they are in the state of an icchantika, they give rise to afflictions such as craving; these afflictions produce karma, and the fruits induced by that karma have not yet been experienced. From the time they begin their practice onward, a vast period of time elapses, and as their merit and wisdom become increasingly profound and expansive, they overshadow the power of their prior causes until it becomes weak; thus, even if other conditions are present, they cannot produce the fruit.
The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states:
"The ninety-eight delusions give rise to a single affliction, and a single affliction gives rise to the ninety-eight delusions.
For example, as when greed fully gives rise to the ninety-eight delusions, all of them are capable of giving rise to greed."
Third, due to the loss of the proper time (*kāla*), even if other conditions are present, the sprout will not arise; for example, seeds sown in spring grow, whereas those sown in winter do not.
Likewise, when the cause loses its proper time, it cannot produce a fruit. For instance, Aṅgulimāla took two thousand lives due to ignorance and would have inevitably entered hell after death;
yet, in his current life, he attained arhatship. Because the timing of his prior evil deeds had shifted, even though other conditions were present, they could no longer produce their fruit.
Fourth, if the causal conditions are not complete, even though the seed is not broken, has not been stored overnight, and the timing is not lost, it will still not sprout.
For example, if the causal conditions such as earth, water, and human effort are incomplete, the sprout cannot be produced.

The same applies to a cause producing its fruit: although it has not yet been destroyed, has not passed a long duration, and has not lost its timing, if the causal conditions are incomplete, it cannot produce the fruit.
If the karma created by sentient beings is capable of drawing forth its resultant fruit, three conditions must be fulfilled:
first, associating with virtuous friends; second, possessing a mind of faith and aspiration; and third, exerting effort through unwholesome actions.
One must seek this by correlating it with three factors; if these three factors are absent, the conditions are incomplete and one cannot obtain the fruit. Thus, the *Vairūpya-sūtra* states:
"If sentient beings wish to be born among humans, yet the causal conditions for their karma are incomplete, they will consequently experience the fruit among animals and other realms."
If one commits evil karma, one ought to be reborn among animals and the like; however, due to the lack of necessary conditions, the fruit is instead experienced among human beings.

This is like an Arhat, who, although possessing various karmas, has exhausted those karmas by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*); because he lacks the accompaniment of afflictions, [the karma] cannot pull forth rebirth.

Furthermore, it is like the Anāgāmin who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): because his karma has been exhausted while his craving has not yet been exhausted, he does not undergo rebirth in the form realm, but is born within the intermediate state.

Furthermore, just as when one attains the first fruit [of the path], although one subsequently gives rise to afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga-prahātavya-kleśa) and these afflictions produce karma—thus possessing both karma and afflictions—one does not again undergo rebirth through the use of new karma, because the afflictions to be destroyed by the path of seeing (darśanamārga-prahātavya-kleśa) have been severed.
Regarding the principle of seeds in the world, it must possess four conditions for a sprout to arise.
It is the same with craving and karma as the principle of seeds: they must likewise possess four conditions to produce a fruit; because they produce a fruit, they are called causes.
Question:
Between karma and afflictions, which one truly serves as the seed? Answer:
Afflictions are primary.
Afflictions give rise to karma, but karma cannot give rise to afflictions, because afflictions are the root.
Furthermore, where there is karma but no affliction, it necessarily cannot pull forth rebirth.
There are afflictions without karma, by virtue of obtaining the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
It is called "arising" (*samudaya*) because two things manifest.

There are two meanings to this manifestation: first, craving and karma correspond to bring about the production of a fruit; while the fruit has not yet arisen, it is not manifest, but at the time of its arising, it becomes manifest.
Second, craving can manifest objects; although objects are in reality base and evil, craving turns the mind to regard objects as good, thereby manifesting objects as being good.

Suppose there is a woman whom three types of beings observe with their respective consciousnesses: an ordinary person sees her as an object of desire; a tiger or wolf views her as food; and a sage regards her as a collection of bones.
That it is perceived as a collection of bones is knowing the object as it is designated;
that it is perceived as something desirable or edible is likewise due to the manifestation of this object through craving.
Due to the manifestation of craving, one gives rise to attachment toward the circumstances of the place where birth is to occur; thus, karma attains its fruit.
If these two manifestations were absent, the fruit could not arise.
To explain the meaning of "arising through accumulation," these two types of manifestation are clarified.
The non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena arise from only a single cause, asserting that the god Īśvara alone is the single cause that produces all things.
Now, in order to refute this view, it is clarified that a fruit can only arise when a multitude of conditions assembles.

Although a multitude of conditions may assemble, if they cannot cause the fruit to arise, they do not possess the nature of a cause; only when their assembly causes the fruit to arise do they qualify as causes.

The two types of manifestation also clarify the meaning of "gathering" (*samudaya*) and clarify the meaning of "causing the fruit to arise"; thus, "manifestation" (*pratibhāsa*) is used as an explanation for "arising through gathering.
It is like a potter, where the various conditions such as the clay, the string, and the water gather together to produce a single jar.
It is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*) because it can extract the fruit and bring it to fulfillment.
While the cause directly induces the fruit to arise, the condition enables the fruit to be born, ensuring that the retribution of a single lifetime is fully and completely accomplished.
Next, the four names of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) are explained.
It is called "cessation" because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are exhausted and do not arise; this is stated with reference to karmic retribution (*vipāka*).
Since the present five aggregates are exhausted and future five aggregates do not arise, it is termed "cessation."
Now, the designation "cessation" (nirodha) merely refers to the essence of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The Truth of Cessation itself takes the unconditioned as its essence; it does not take the cessation and non-arising of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) as its essence.

While the cessation and non-arising of the five aggregates pertain to the three periods of time, the essence of the Truth of Cessation is unconditioned and is therefore not a phenomenon belonging to the three periods of time.

Regarding the statement that the cessation and non-arising of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) pertains to the three periods of time: the five aggregates of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others have already ceased and do not arise in the past;
the five aggregates of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) will only cease and not arise in the future;
and the five aggregates of noble ones (ārya) in the present are ceasing and not arising in the present.

Within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there are no five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the five aggregates do not arise therein. Therefore, the meaning of "exhaustion" and "non-arising" is used to designate the unconditioned.
Furthermore, it is only when the five aggregates have been extinguished and do not arise that one realizes this unconditioned state.
Because the meaning of the exhaustion of non-arising characterizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the unconditioned is termed "cessation" (*nirodha*).
It is called "tranquility" (*śānta*) because it can extinguish the three fires.
There are two kinds of these three fires:
First, desire, hatred, and delusion constitute the three fires.
These three are called "fires" for three reasons:

first, they can burn away all the roots of goodness in sentient beings; second, these three afflictions cause the mind to become feverish, which carries the sense of burning the mind; and third, they can ignite the three realms, and are therefore called fires.
These three afflictions pervade the three realms and arise from the six objects, the six faculties, and the six consciousnesses.
These afflictions, as well as their roots, objects, and consciousnesses, are all with-outflows (*sāsrava*); because of these three afflictions, one cannot attain peace and happiness.
The three afflictions are like fire that can burn; the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are like fuel, which are what is burned.
Question:
Since there is no anger (*dveṣa*) in the higher realms, how can it now be said that anger exists there?
Answer:

Ordinary beings born in the higher realms possess the afflictions of seeing the truths (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); they are not absent in those higher realms, but because they cannot arise there, it is said that they do not exist.
What is now called "existence" is spoken of from the perspective of ultimate principle.
Second, the three types of suffering are treated as three fires.

These three sufferings can burn sentient beings so that they find no peace or happiness: in the desire realm all three sufferings are present; in the form realm, there are the two sufferings of change and conditioning; and in the formless realm, there is only the suffering of conditioning.

The three types of suffering are the three calamities: the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) is the fire calamity, the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā) is the water calamity, and the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā) is the wind calamity.

When these two kinds of triple fires are present, there is agitation; because these two kinds of triple fires are extinguished, it is called "tranquil" (śānta), and because the three injustices are absent, it is called "sublime" (praṇīta).
The three oppressions refer to birth, old age, and death as the three sufferings.
Because these three sufferings are equally pervasive throughout the three realms, these three specifically are designated as the three oppressions.
All three realms possess birth; therefore, there is the suffering of birth.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is old age characterized by white hair and wrinkled faces. Although the six heavens and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) lack these physical manifestations of aging, they nonetheless possess the principle of transformation and decline. For example, a painting is clear and lovely when first created, but over time its colors fade and thin; the material bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the higher realms are likewise subject to this principle, which is precisely what is termed "old age."

The mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) likewise undergoes aging; as its karmic fruition (*vipāka*) is about to end, the functioning of the mind undergoes transformation. Whereas previously the concentrated mind was firm and stable, as it nears its conclusion, the concentrated mind becomes weak and inferior, constantly tending toward decline and falling away.
Therefore, all three realms possess the suffering of old age.
All three realms possess an end, and thus all possess the suffering of death.

The reason these are called "wrongs" (*wang*) is that the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is to constantly seek peace and happiness; they cultivate worldly virtues in the hope of obtaining a pleasant retribution, yet these three calamities of untimely death cause them to suffer. Hence, the three types of suffering are termed the "three wrongs."
Within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these three types of injustice do not exist; therefore, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*).
Question:
When one is born in the higher realms, there is no suffering for oneself; why then is it called "suffering"?
Answer: It is not necessarily the case that it is called suffering because it gives rise to painful sensations; rather, it is called suffering because its arising is the root of suffering.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not arise, and therefore it has no suffering; birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) involves arising, and therefore it has suffering. For this reason, birth is designated as suffering.
Just as "hell" (naraka) is a name for a location, yet the location itself is not actually suffering; rather, because the location can give rise to suffering, hell is called suffering.
Question:
As for the arising of suffering, among the three types of suffering, which one is it?

Answer: If suffering arises, it is the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā); if pleasure arises, it is the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā); if equanimity arises, it is the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
Birth in the desire realm possesses all three types of suffering.

Birth in the form realm possesses two types of suffering, namely the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*) and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkha*); in the formless realm, there is only the suffering of conditioned formations.

The suffering of old age also possesses all three types of suffering: if it transforms pleasure into suffering, it is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkha*); if it transforms suffering into pleasure or transforms pleasure into pleasure, it is the suffering of change; and if it transforms pleasure into equanimity, it is the suffering of conditioned formations.
By analogy with the three realms, this suffering of death also possesses the three types of suffering; it can be understood by comparison with what preceded.
Question:
How many types of suffering are spoken of in the sutras?
Answer: It is said that there are immeasurable sufferings.

Apart from the eight types of suffering mentioned here, when analyzed in detail, there are further various sufferings; however, [in this context] we have merely limited ourselves to describing seven types of suffering.
Among the traditional eight sufferings, the suffering of illness is not mentioned; rather, after enumerating seven sufferings, it states "and so forth" to include all other sufferings.

The reason the suffering of illness is not mentioned is that this suffering exists only among humans in the desire realm and is not pervasive throughout the heavens of the desire realm; therefore, it is not included.
The reason why there is no suffering from illness among the gods is that illness arises from internal and external conditions.
"External" refers to imbalances such as cold and heat, or the lack of moderation in food and drink; thus, it causes the suffering of illness.

Internally, some may walk excessively and cause the four great elements to weaken, or sit excessively and cause the four great elements to weaken; because the four great elements have weakened, illness arises.

In the higher realms, there are no external conditions such as the imbalance of cold and heat or the lack of moderation in food and drink; since the internal four great elements are already strong and there are no conditions of excessive walking or sitting, they cannot suffer from the pain of illness.
There is also the sense that "misinterpretation" constitutes illness.

When the gods of the six heavens engage in sexual desire, they may abstain from food for three days or even up to seven days; if they do not eat by the seventh day, they die. Even before death, their four great elements (mahābhūta) become weak, which can also be termed the suffering of illness.
Question:
What are the remaining four types of suffering? Answer:
If the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) pertain to all three realms, there are the sufferings of seeking what one cannot obtain, separation from the beloved, and encountering the hated.

These three types of suffering are definitively absent in the two higher realms; because they abide solely in the fruition of their own names and do not dwell together in a mixed state, these three sufferings do not exist there.
The six heavens of the desire realm possess all of these.
The gods of the lower grades aspire to the higher grades; because they cannot attain them, suffering arises—this is precisely the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Engaging in battle with the asuras is the suffering of encountering what one hates.
Failing in battle and being bound or defeated by the asuras is the suffering of separation from what one loves.
Because one is liberated from all losses, it is called "eternal departure.
All losses consist of causes, conditions, and retributive fruits.
Causes are afflictions; conditions are karma; and that which is received—the five aggregates—is the retributive fruit. These three are dharmas of fault.
One is ultimately liberated from these three; it is not a temporary liberation, and is therefore called "perpetual departure.
Question:
Why is affliction termed the cause and karma termed the condition?
Answer: Afflictions are the seeds that are truly capable of drawing forth rebirth; therefore, they are called the cause.
If there were no afflictions, even if karma were present, it would be unable to draw forth rebirth.
If there were no karma but only afflictions, one could still arise in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
However, if afflictions are exhausted, although karma may produce a magnificent fruit, it is ultimately because karma is produced by afflictions that the fruit is obtained.
Next, the four names of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) are explained.
It is called the "Path" (*mārga*) because one proceeds (*yāti*) by means of it.
There are two explanations for this:

One explanation states that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are the "practitioner," while morality, concentration, and wisdom are the "practice.

From the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) up to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvayajñāna*), the twelve moments of mind all constitute the knowledge of exhaustion because they sever the afflictions; the thirteenth moment of mind is the knowledge of non-arising.
Precepts may be with outflows (*sāsrava*) by nature, yet they become without outflows (*anāsrava*) through the practice of two types of knowledge.
The same applies to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
There are three kinds of knowledge: that derived from hearing (*śruta*), reflection (*cintā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) is also both with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and without-outflow (*anāsrava*). It becomes without-outflow because it is practiced by means of two types of knowledge.
When practiced by means of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of the outflow of suffering (*duḥkhasrotas-jñāna*) manifests, and one is endowed with the eightfold noble path.

Precepts and concentration are originally with outflows (*sāsrava*); now, because they are practiced for the sake of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they become without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This knowledge of exhaustion is of two kinds: first, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and second, right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).

Although both contemplate impermanence, there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle: right view is subtle and right thought is coarse; yet these two can mutually give rise to one another.

If one takes right view to be the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one may also say that it causes right view to become untainted (*anāsrava*); ultimately, it is by means of the knowledge of exhaustion that wisdom is made untainted.
When explained in this way, they are simultaneously the objects of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); thus, morality, concentration, and wisdom become untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because their natures are distinct, they can exist at the same time; this applies to all [stages] up to the Arhat.

If one were to compare right view with right view, or right thought with right thought, they could not exist simultaneously; rather, it must be that the preceding right view causes the subsequent right view to become free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Right reflection is likewise; it cannot exist simultaneously, because two dharmas of a single nature cannot coexist.

If this principle is clarified in this way, then the wisdom of clarity at different times constitutes the sphere of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and so on, up to the Arhat—all are thus;
it constitutes the sphere of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and so on, up to the Arhat—all are thus.

Regarding the statement that "precepts, concentration, and wisdom become untainted (anāsrava) through the practice of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna)": after the vision of the truths (satyadarśana), there are ten subsequent moments of mind; these ten subsequent minds belong to the fruit.

If a person on the stage of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) performs the contemplation of twelve moments of mind, then the precepts, concentration, and wisdom occurring simultaneously with the knowledge of non-arising, as well as the wisdom occurring at a different time, become untainted.
Question:
Is the vision of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) not itself the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); why, then, is it not so described? Answer:

If the vision of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) is considered in relation to the subsequent knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna*), it may also be termed "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*);
if it is viewed in relation to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*), it serves as its basis;
and in its function of severing the afflictions of the higher realms, it further belongs to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Since it is not definitively the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), it is entirely subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Only the thirteenth moment of mind is definitive; therefore, it can be called the knowledge of non-arising.

Regarding the second interpretation, it states that morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the "path" (*mārga*) because they are accomplished through the activity of the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*). Thus, the untainted mind is the agent of activity (*kartṛ*), while morality, concentration, and wisdom are the objects of activity (*karman*); this is because the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that assist the mind.

The previous explanation differs from the subsequent interpretation. Regarding the statement "within [them]," if one discusses this generally, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*) because it accords with the principle that corresponds to the four [foundations]. If one discusses it specifically, it is called "suchness" because it accords with the principle of the middle way, which is neither eternal nor annihilated.
When the wisdom that realizes suchness is not subverted by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), it cannot be rendered "not-as-it-is" (*tathatā*); therefore, it is called "suchness.
Because it is produced by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), it is called "right practice" (*samyakpratipatti*).

If a śrāvaka hears the correct teaching from a true teacher, and from those correct sounds and names gives rise to correct hearing, and from correct hearing gives rise to correct cultivation—practicing and learning in this sequential order is called "that which is to be done."

If it concerns Pratyekabuddhas or Buddhas, then right cultivation arises from right reflection; there is no case where the meaning of right hearing arises from the sound of right names, because the faculties of these two vehicles are so sharp that they are able to attain awakening through their own independent reflection.
Question:

Since both Pratyekabuddhas and Buddhas have previously heard the Dharma throughout their fundamental existences, thereby giving rise to the wisdom of reflection and cultivation, why is it that they do not give rise to correct reflection from correct hearing?
Answer: It is not that you have not heard of this in previous lives.
This present discussion concerns actual events; it is not merely a recollection of what was heard in the past.

At that time, the teacher makes this statement and relies upon this statement; based on this, one gives rise to wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), contemplating directly and uprightly until one personally attains realization of the principle.
A *śrāvaka*, however, must necessarily contemplate by relying on the words of the teacher.
It is called "renunciation" (niḥsaraṇa) because it eternally transcends [suffering].
There are two interpretations.
One interpretation states:
Due to wrong reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), afflictions arise; from afflictions, karma arises; and from karma, retribution arises—all of these are due to improper reflection.
If untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) arises, then from that wisdom, morality, meditative concentration, and so forth arise; all of these are correct.
The correct (*samyak*) is the opposite of the incorrect (*asamyak*); "correct" here refers to an excessive degree of correctness, not merely a temporary excess, but one that is permanent.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds:
afflictions (*kleśa*) are inverted, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is non-inverted.
Inversion is the opposite of non-inversion; non-inversion eternally transcends inversion.
The former explanation is extensive, while the latter is concise; thus, they have different functions.
Furthermore, the former school offers another interpretation of the sixteen names, stating that because it is not an eternal dharma-nature, it is called "impermanent."
If unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) were inherently existent from the beginning, they would never arise, never abide, and never cease.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), by contrast, arise momentarily, abide momentarily, and cease momentarily; such is the nature of these phenomena, and therefore they are called impermanent (*anitya*).
Because it arises from ignorance, one who suffers does not understand worldly affairs.
If suffering is itself already a state of suffering due to the failure to understand worldly affairs, how much more so is it for one who fails to understand the true, profound principle?

This is indeed great suffering; ignorance is the root of suffering. Because one undergoes the retribution of birth and death due to ignorance, there is no place within birth and death that is not suffering.
It is called "emptiness" because it is devoid of a person in the interim.
The six sense faculties are the "intermediate. The Buddha himself used the analogy of a village to represent the six sense faculties.
What is now called the "intermediate" is like the space within a village.
Since the self and persons do not exist within this intermediate space, it is said to be "separated from persons."
It is called "emptiness" because it is devoid of self and person.
Regarding the statement that it is called "non-self" because of a lack of sovereignty, there are two meanings to sovereignty:
first, it is called sovereignty because of not depending on another; if something does not arise, abide, or cease through another, then it is sovereign.

Second, it is called "mastery" because one acts according to one's will; if one wishes to make fire cold, the fire immediately becomes cold, and if one wishes to make water non-wet, the water immediately becomes non-wet—this is mastery.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are dependent upon others; therefore, they possess arising, abiding, and ceasing, and furthermore, they cannot be obtained according to one's wishes.

Even if one possesses supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) capable of transformation, such functions can only arise after one has necessarily relied upon the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and other practices. Since they cannot escape dependence, there is no autonomy (*svatantrya*); and since there is no autonomy, there is no self (*ātman*).
Because it brings about the principle [of arising], it is called a "cause" (*hetu*). Next, I shall provide an analogy in sequence to explain this.
The seed is used as the analogy.

For instance, when a seed exists, it possesses the inherent power to produce a tree even without depending on other conditions; although the tree has not yet arisen, because the seed already possesses the power to produce, it can cause the sprout and subsequent stages to emerge at a later time.
Present karma is divided into four parts. As for the first part:

at the time when one performs wholesome or unwholesome actions, they possess an inherent power to induce results even without depending on other conditions; this result remains in the future until the end of one's life.
Since karma possesses the power to induce a fruit, it can cause that fruit to arrive at a later time.
Because there exists a principle by which what is present can cause something to come, the principle of "coming" is termed a "cause."

Regarding the statement that it is called "arising" (samudaya) because it emerges through a causal principle: the seed has the inherent capacity to produce a tree; the sprout, stem, branches, leaves, and so forth originally exist in the future. Now, when the seed is placed within the soil and relies upon external conditions such as earth and water, the sprout finally emerges. As soon as the sprout arises in the present, the seed immediately perishes.
Karma is also like this: its nature is inherently to induce a fruit, which exists in the future.

Once the present retribution is exhausted, one first undergoes birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); as soon as karma is initiated within that intermediate birth, its initial portion immediately passes away.

There exists a principle by which karma can emerge from the intermediate state (antarābhava); however, the fruit of the intermediate state arises only when causes and conditions converge. Therefore, because it is said that there is a principle for its emergence, it is called "arising through accumulation" (samudaya).

Regarding the phrase "the stage of development is called the place of birth": first, the sprout appears; from the sprout grows the stalk. From the initial emergence of the stalk until just before the flower has formed, this period is termed the stage of development.
As the practitioner gradually progresses, they pass through the stage of the sprout; as the stalk barely emerges, the sprout then withers.

Karma is likewise: first one experiences the sprout of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), then, relinquishing the sprout of the intermediate state, one undergoes actual birth. From the initial *kalala* stage until the end of the seventh division, this is called "progressing through the stages of becoming."

It is called "action" (*saṃskāra*) because it gradually increases; it is called "passing over" (*gati*) because it transcends the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The karma that brings about the mere arising of the *kalala* ceases at its second stage.

It is called "birth" (*jāti*) because the *kalala* and subsequent stages arise in succession; it is called "karma" because this birth arises from karma. Because it serves as the basis for these states, it is called "action-passing-over" (*gati-saṃskāra*), and thus it is termed "karma of the place of birth."
The third part concerns their own inherent power.
If there were no karmic efficacy, then even if other conditions were present to produce a fruit, it would ultimately never arise.
Because they serve as the basis for this principle, they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*).

The initial gradual growth of the stalk before the flower has yet emerged, from the time the flower appears until the fruit is formed, and the subsequent production of a future tree from that fruit—all these are termed the principle of dependence (*āśraya-yukti*).
Flowers, fruits, and so forth all arise based on the seeds of this stage;
as soon as the flower has produced the seed, the third part [of the process] ceases.
Karma is likewise: from the initial *kalala* stage up to the seventh part, it is unable to act as the cause for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) or for liberation.
From the second moment after the six sense faculties are fully developed onwards, one is able to create the causes for saṃsāra and liberation; this stage constitutes the fourth part of karma.
From the beginning of this fourth part onwards, whether it be suffering or pleasure, evil or good, all depend upon this fourth part of karma.
The fourth part of karma is called a "condition" because it relies upon principle;
as soon as the fourth part of karma arises, the third part of karma ceases.

While the fourth part of karma is itself powerful in its own function, once the fruit has already arisen, its reliance on other conditions becomes weak; it is precisely due to the activity of the karma that the fruit attains completion.

If the second portion of karma produces birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), both the cause and the condition are weak; since craving serves as the cause and karma as the condition, both factors are feeble. Therefore, it cannot be fully illustrated by the analogy of a seed; the analogy applies only in part.
When karma is being performed, it possesses the capacity to induce these four states; as the fruits manifest according to their respective times, there are these four types.
It is with reference to these states that karma is divided into four categories.
Question:
How can a single karma suddenly bring about these various fruits simultaneously? Answer:
Regarding a single moment of clarity within a single karma, it may likewise be analyzed into three parts: the initial and final parts are weak, while the central part of clarity is strong.
The weak parts induce the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), while the strong part induces the fruit of rebirth.
If it concerns uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma, then it is strong at the beginning and weak at the end.
Question:
How does the production of a fruit by karma differ from that of a seed?
Answer: This point is not the same.

If one follows schools such as the Sarvāstivāda, which clarify that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*), then for a single seed, we shall speak on the basis of ten moments.

If one discusses the production of characteristics according to their respective divisions, the first moment can produce the second moment, and the second moment can produce the third; thus, they are always clearly shown to produce one another in immediate succession.
The first [moment] arises and immediately perishes; it does not reach the second [moment], so how could it produce the third?

If one speaks in terms of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) from the perspective of its preceding portion and in relation to the continuity (*saṃtati*), then the homogeneous cause of the first moment is able to produce everything from the second moment onward, up to the flower and fruit; this homogeneous cause subsumes these karmic fruits within the future.
The first moment perishes; the second moment’s homogeneous state (*sabhāga*) encompasses the results from the third moment onward within the future, and subsequent stages follow this same pattern.
If the seed of the first moment were not present as the basis, then the second and third moments could not exist, because they must follow in successive succession.
Therefore, it is said that the seed of the initial moment is capable of producing [the subsequent moments].

Regarding the subsequent mention of "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*) among the various effects: the seeds and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute the four parts; because they are equally capable of producing a single effect, they bear this name.
This is not like the case of karma, where the "possession of similarity" (*sabhāgata*) subsumes both cause and effect.
If one follows the Saṃmitīya school, matter does not perish moment by moment, but possesses the quality of abiding for a brief duration.
When the seed has not yet produced the sprout, it is merely a single seed.
If one discusses the production of fruits according to their specific parts, it refers specifically to the production of the sprout.
If one considers the continuum, there is also the sense of producing the stem, leaves, and so forth; subsequent categories are all like this.
Karma is not like this; although karma itself perishes, there remains the "dharma of non-loss" which retains its fruit so that it is not lost.
For now, let us speak in terms of the wholesome karma of the precepts.
The precepts have a foundation; that foundation consists of the preliminary preparations (*pūrvakṛtya*) and the actual preparations (*sammukhībhāva*).

The preliminary preparations comprise three matters: first, the harmony of the assembly granting permission for the reception of the precepts; second, the formal request for the precepts; and third, the proper time.
Regarding the time: it is the commitment to cease all evil for as long as one lives.

Regarding the correct method: the teacher performs the ritual of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tri-karman*); upon the completion of the third proclamation, one immediately attains the protection of body and speech.

This goodness is itself the precept; it is gathered by means of conditions such as the resolve of the mind, which serves as its foundation. It remains undiminished for as long as one lives, and from that point onward, it flows continuously in succession.
If one commits an offense during the interim, the precepts no longer flow; however, once the confession is completed, they flow forth again.
To say they "flow" means they flow out from the root.

That which flows forth from the wholesome precept of a single moment arises and ceases immediately; it does not produce a second moment of precept from that first moment, but rather a second moment of precept flows forth again from the root. In this way, subsequent productions are able to flow forth from the root.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there is a "concomitant acquisition" (*prāpti*) that follows along with it.
Although the wholesome precept has passed away, its concomitant acquisition remains bound in the past, while its binding of the fruit exists in the future.
According to the Saṃmitīya school, when wholesome precepts give rise to this wholesome karma, they arise together with the *avipraṇāśa-dharma* (the factor of non-disappearance).

They do not assert that there is a functional capacity (*śakti*) within the karma; rather, as soon as the essence of the karma arises, it immediately perishes. However, the *avipraṇāśa-dharma* does not perish, and it retains the fruit of the karma so that it is not lost.

It is not a dharma that perishes moment by moment; rather, it is a dharma that perishes dependent upon time. It possesses the sense of abiding for a while, and its substance only passes away when the arising of a fruit is awaited.
If it were a fixed precept, it would possess the quality of continuing to flow in accordance with its fundamental basis.
However, the substance of a gift continues to flow as a wholesome state in accordance with that object; if it were not a wholesome state that flows, one could not obtain the fruit [of the gift].

There is no such thing as an "indestructible dharma" (avipraṇāśa-dharma) that arises simultaneously with a wholesome [state], nor is there any sense in which it persists as a constant, uncontaminated (anāsrava) wholesome flow within other subsequent minds.
Question:
Since the karma and the indestructible dharma arise together and are both conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), why does the essence of the karma perish while the indestructible dharma does not?
Answer: Wholesome states are mental concomitants; therefore, they arise and immediately perish.
Non-defiled states are not mental concomitants; therefore, they do not perish moment by moment.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the "attainment by following" (*anuprāpti*) likewise perishes moment by moment; however, it is not of the same category as mind-associated dharmas, and its own continuum remains uninterrupted.
Question:
How is the constant flow of the wholesome [state] of giving (*dāna*) established?
Answer: Body and speech constitute the substance of karma; physical gestures are taken as bodily karma, and verbal expressions are taken as vocal karma.

Moving the hands to grasp an object—whether picking it up, lifting it, or offering it to another person—is precisely what constitutes a physical gesture; it is by means of these gestures that bodily karma is established.
To utter words such as "I shall take such-and-such an object and give it to such-and-such a person" constitutes verbal karma (*vākkarman*).
There are three conditions for the arising of bodily and verbal karma:
first, the three wholesome roots (*trīṇi kuśalamūlāni*).
Second, from the three roots of goodness arises right reflection;
third, from right reflection arises mental attention (*manasikāra*), namely, the intention to give.
Generally speaking, these three conditions give rise to physical and vocal karma.
Regarding the proximate treatise: it is precisely through mental attention (*manasikāra*) that bodily and vocal karma are initiated.
As for what is called "giving" (*dāna*), because one initiates bodily and vocal karma by means of three conditions, it is termed the virtue of giving.
The Bodhisattva silently contemplates and rains down jewels; thus, mental action is also an act of giving.
There are three kinds of fields:
first, the field of merit, such as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Second is the field of nurturance, such as one's parents;
third is the field of the destitute, namely sentient beings suffering from hunger and cold.
If one gives to the field of merit, then non-delusive roots of goodness will be abundant.
If one gives to the field of the poor, there is no lack of the roots of goodness of non-delusion and non-hatred, because one necessarily arouses compassion toward impoverished sentient beings.

There is an abundance of the root of goodness of non-hatred; thus, within a single moment, all three roots of goodness are present. However, depending on the specific field to which they are directed, there are differences in their relative degree.
Giving is further of two kinds:
first, giving out of reverence; second, giving for the sake of benefit.
If it is giving out of reverence, it is wholesome at the time of giving, but once the giving is finished, it no longer flows forth.
The reason for this is as follows: it is like making offerings of clothing, food, and so forth out of reverence for the Buddha even after he has entered parinirvāṇa;
it is also like how people of the world make offerings of clothing, food, and so forth to World-Honored Ones of the past, likewise out of reverence.
Since no one is there to enjoy these things, merit cannot flow accordingly with the act. Second is the gift for the benefit [of others]:
it is for the sake of benefiting the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the recipient, because by their enjoying these things, their four great elements are increased.
When giving for the sake of benefit, goodness flows continuously through three factors.
These three factors are: first, the three roots of goodness;
second, other things; [and third, the recipient].
Third, regarding sentient beings:
if any one of these three factors is incomplete, the wholesome flow no longer continues.

For example, even if other things are not yet exhausted and sentient beings continue to use them, if the donor has already died, or has given rise to wrong views and severed their roots of goodness, then because the wholesome no longer has a foundation, it does not flow forth again.

If the donor is still living, their roots of goodness are not severed, and the recipient continues to exist, yet the remaining goods have been exhausted, then the flow of merit will no longer continue.

If the donor has not severed their roots of goodness and has not died, and other goods have not yet been exhausted, yet the person who was able to enjoy and use them has passed away and ceased to exist, such that no one remains to enjoy them, then the merit will no longer flow.
Although others may use it, this was not what the donor originally intended; thus, the recipient merely enjoys it in vain, and no merit will accrue at the end.
However, if the donor’s intention for giving was universal, then whatever use is made of the gift will result in the accumulation of merit.

Therefore, when those who serve as fields of merit receive offerings from others, they must establish certain restrictions; if they permit the use of the gifts according to one's own will, then the merit generated through successive acts of dedication will be inexhaustible.

If one does not do so, but instead diverts the gift to another, one violates the intention of the donor; such a person who diverts the offering not only gains no merit but further incurs sin, and will eventually fall into the evil realms to undergo mutual retribution.
This is not easy; therefore, one should be cautious regarding it.
Question:
Once the roots of goodness have been severed, and since goodness no longer has a basis, how can goodness arise once more?
Answer: This should be further questioned in two ways.

Since the first path of the *srotāpanna* is untainted (*anāsrava*) and lacks any untainted category as its fundamental basis, how can one claim that an Arhat, through falling away, gives rise to the afflictions destroyed by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
If afflictions do not have unwholesome roots as their basis, how can they arise?
Answer: There are two kinds of causes for arising: first, the cause of prior arising; second, the cause of simultaneous arising.

The "pre-arising cause" (pūrvotpannahetu) refers to these three roots of goodness; because they exist prior to the performance of a wholesome deed and are capable of generating that deed, they are called the pre-arising cause.

As for the co-nascent cause (*sahaja-hetu*), it is because wholesome states arise through the mental application of discernment (*manasikāra-vicaya*); since the very moment of discernment is the moment of their arising as wholesome, it is called the co-nascent cause.
If the roots of goodness have not been severed, when performing wholesome deeds, they arise from two causes;
if the roots of goodness have already been severed, when performing wholesome deeds, they arise solely from the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
When the roots of goodness arise again, they reconnect with the three roots of goodness, causing them to be associated with wholesome states of mind.

The severance of the roots of goodness does not mean that the essence of these roots is completely extinguished; rather, because they are obstructed by wrong views, wholesome states of mind no longer associate with them, and this is termed "severance."
If the untainted path arises, the substance of the tainted roots of goodness is extinguished.
In the initial untainted path of the *srotāpanna*, there were previously no untainted roots of goodness; they arise solely from co-nascence (*sahaja*).

When an Arhat regresses and gives rise to afflictions, although the three unwholesome roots have already been exhausted, these [afflictions] arise solely from the cause of co-nascence (*sahaja-hetu*).
Question:
When the Buddha of the Lesser Vehicle accepts an offering of food, does he defecate or urinate while eating this food?
Answer: The Buddha has no excrement or urine.

On both sides beneath the Buddha’s jaw, extending toward the neck, there are a thousand sinews that receive the flavor of all food. Once the food reaches this place, it is transformed into blood and flesh; therefore, there is no excrement or urine.
Regarding the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), there are two interpretations:
one says he has excrement and urine; the other says he does not.
As for the Three Vehicles, they are the same as ordinary beings in that they also have excrement and urine.

The food of the six heavens is called *sūdā*; *su* is translated as "good" (*śubha*) and *dā* is translated as "pure and real. This food is so refined and subtle that it does not produce excrement or urine.
The meaning of "extinction" (*nirodha*) is the absence of common bondage; because common bondage is completely purified and exhausted, it is called extinction.

Generally, there should only be the latter term, yet where the former term also occurs, the Indic language calls it *nilodha*. This single name has ten meanings: concealment is also called *nilodha*, hiding is also called *nilodha*, and cessation is also called *nilodha*.
Since this passage now demonstrates and explains the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*) rather than other meanings, it is analyzed by means of the first phrase.
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama* (specifically the *Vimokṣa-sūtra*), the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Craving resides within your eyes; you must extinguish it."
If craving is extinguished, your eye is also extinguished; for it is due to the eye encountering forms that craving arises, which together bind consciousness.
Craving is the bondage of afflictions, while the eye and its objective realm of forms are the objects of that bondage.
If the fetters of craving are extinguished, the fetters of the eye and so forth are likewise destroyed.
A sutra illustrates this by saying: "It is like using a chain to bind a person and cast them into a prison."
The chain is one bondage; the prison is another bondage.
If one strikes away the chain and incinerates the prison, then one is liberated from these two bondages.
Because both bondages together bind sentient beings, they are called "jointly bound."

It is called "pure" because it is liberated from craving; it is called "exhausted" because it is liberated from objective spheres. This constitutes both *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
The cessation of craving is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; the cessation of objective spheres is *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, and the rest.
It is called "tranquility" because of liberation from the three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the three characteristics of the conditioned, there are two types: first, the three time periods as the three characteristics of the conditioned; second, birth, aging, and cessation as the three characteristics of the conditioned.

The reason why it is not said that there is "abiding" is that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have no abiding; abiding is a characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and therefore it is not mentioned [in relation to them].

Through wrong reflection (*mithyā-manasikāra*), afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; from afflictions, karma (*karman*) is produced; and from karma, retribution (*vipāka*) arises. Since there is thus a mutual production of cause and effect, the three periods of time (*traiyadhvika*) exist.
Because unconditioned phenomena lack this mutual production of cause and effect, they do not possess the three periods of time.
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are originally non-existent and thus have arising; because they have arising, they have aging and cessation.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are originally existent and thus have no arising; because they have no arising, they have no aging or cessation.
Conditioned phenomena possess two kinds of three characteristics; because they are agitated and restless, they are not tranquil.
Unconditioned phenomena are liberated from these two kinds of three characteristics; since they lack agitation and restlessness, they are called tranquil.
For each single affliction there is one liberation; for the ninety-eight afflictions, there are ninety-eight liberations.
All dharmas are originally unarisen; that which is unarisen is liberation.

Because sentient beings are subject to inversion, they give rise to craving and attachment toward form and other phenomena; due to this craving and attachment, karma is produced, and from karma, retribution arises.
When afflictions crave and attach to form, they cannot accord with the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that they face.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that serves as the counteragent is precisely this [cessation]; once this craving is severed, one realizes this unconditioned state. Therefore, for each of the ninety-eight afflictions, there is a corresponding unconditioned state; the same applies to karma and its retribution.
Regarding afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no separate unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entity.
Because it is truly wholesome, it is called "sublime" (*praṇīta*).
Wholesomeness itself is of four kinds: first, true wholesomeness; second, natural wholesomeness; third, concomitant wholesomeness; and fourth, originating wholesomeness.
Ultimate goodness is precisely nirvāṇa.
Saṃsāra consists of unwholesome dharmas, whereas nirvāṇa is devoid of evil; because it does not arise from causes and conditions, it is called ultimate goodness.
That which is wholesome by nature consists of the three roots of goodness: non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
These three roots of goodness do not depend on other conditions; their very nature is capable of counteracting the three unwholesome states of attachment, hatred, and delusion.
Nirvāṇa is free from the three evil realms; because it accords with the nature of nirvāṇa, it is called "wholesome.
It is like three medicinal herbs that do not depend on external conditions, yet by their inherent nature can cure diseases:
oil can cure wind-disorders, ghee can cure heat-disorders, and honey can cure cold-disorders.

Regarding "wholesome through the intermixture of the three characteristics," this refers to the wholesomeness of mental action (*manas-karman*), which arises from its association with the three wholesome roots (*kuśala-mūla*).
When faith, wisdom, and other such qualities arise, the mind and its concomitant mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that are associated with the three wholesome roots all become wholesome.
When they are not yet mixed, each of the three roots of goodness can individually counteract one type of evil.

If the mind and its associated mental factors are not mixed with the three roots of goodness, they lack the capacity to counteract evil; however, when they are mixed, they are able to comprehensively destroy all evils.
Just as various medicines can each cure diseases when they have not yet been mixed together, but once combined, there is no disease they cannot treat.
Fourth, the arousal of the wholesome refers to the wholesomeness of body and speech.
The body and speech are fundamentally not good; it is because wholesome mental karma gives rise to the actions of body and speech that goodness is produced in them.
For example, water is originally not medicine, but when medicine is placed within the water and boiled, the water is activated by the medicine so that the water itself becomes medicine.
The three roots of goodness all become established as good because they accord with true goodness.
Evil is a coarse phenomenon;
the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is devoid of evil and is thus truly good, and for this reason it is called "sublime" (praṇīta).
Question:
When the mind and its associated mental factors are conjoined with the three roots of goodness, are they all simultaneously conjoined with all three roots of goodness?
Answer:
At one time, it is fully associated with the three roots of goodness.
For instance, when faith, wisdom, and so forth manifest, this mind accords with principle, which is itself non-delusion; that greed and hatred do not arise is itself non-greed and non-hatred.
Question:
When the mind and its associated mental factors are associated with the three unwholesome roots, are they simultaneously associated with all three unwholesome roots?
Answer:
When an unwholesome mind manifests, this mind deviates from reason and is constantly associated with ignorance (*avidyā*).
When suffering is associated with greed, it is not associated with hatred, because their natures are diametrically opposed.
Question:
Are the three roots of goodness mental factors? Answer:
Because it is not a mental factor (*caitta*), there are times when it does not associate with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*).
As the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools teach: "The nature of the mind of sentient beings is originally pure, defiled only by adventitious dust."
Purity consists of the three roots of goodness.
Sentient beings have possessed adventitious dust since beginningless birth and death; this is affliction (*kleśa*).
Affliction refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and other such afflictions. These latent dispositions are the three unwholesome roots.

Because the three roots of goodness exist, faith, wisdom, and so forth arise; when faith, wisdom, and so forth arise, they mutually support the three roots of goodness, and are therefore called "associated.

Because the three unwholesome roots exist, greed, hatred, and other unwholesome states are produced; when these unwholesome states arise, they mutually support the three unwholesome roots, and are thus said to be "associated."

If one gives rise to wrong views and severs the three roots of goodness, those three roots are temporarily extinguished but not extinguished forever; later, if wholesome states arise, they reconnect with them and cause them to be born again.
However, if one severs the three unwholesome roots, once severed they never arise again; because they are most excellently stilled, they are called "permanently abandoned."
Just as a person dwelling amidst enemies and bandits cannot find rest;
yet if they sever ties with those enemies and bandits, even though not yet far removed from them, there is the sense of finding rest, though it is not the most supreme rest;
only when one has completely emerged from their domain is it the most supreme rest.
The internal application is likewise: if one remains amidst the enemies and bandits of the afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no peace at all.
Even if one has somewhat severed them, as long as they are not completely eradicated, there is the sense of peace, yet it is not the supreme peace.
Only when they are entirely eradicated and one forever emerges from the realm of the afflictions is this the supreme peace.
The Arhat has exhausted all afflictions and will never give rise to them again; this is the most supreme peace.
The Srotāpanna has exhausted the afflictions regarding the vision of the truths and will never give rise to them again; this, too, is the most supreme peace.
It is called the "Path" because it serves as the antidote to wrong paths.
Among the ninety-six kinds of śramaṇas, all practice wrong paths.
They are termed "wrong paths" because those who travel these paths go nowhere; therefore, they are called wrong paths.
If one practices the straight path of morality, concentration, and wisdom, one will attain nirvana.
To counteract wrong paths, morality, concentration, and wisdom are taught as the path.
Furthermore, it is explained that they are called the "path" (mārga) because they can be sought after.
Just as a person who intends to reach a certain destination must first seek out the road,
so too one who seeks liberation must first seek the supramundane path. Since morality,
concentration, and wisdom are the places where this path is sought, they are called the "path."
It is called "suchness" (tathatā) because it counteracts what is not such.
There are two interpretations:
first, clarifying that it counteracts what is not in accordance with principle; second, clarifying that it counteracts what is not in accordance with practice.

The four inversions are inconsistent with principle and are therefore not suchness; for they place permanence, bliss, self, and purity within saṃsāra, while placing impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity within nirvāṇa.

Now, observing that birth and death are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, while Nirvana is permanent, blissful, self, and pure—to correspond with this principle is precisely Suchness (Tathatā).
Question:
How can the Nirvana of the Hīnayāna be considered "self"?
If this were so, then it would follow that not all phenomena are selfless. Answer:
In the Lesser Vehicle, it is taught that there is no self among all phenomena; for this reason alone, they are called "selfless."
Nirvana possesses a substantial entity; that which possesses a substantial entity is precisely the self of dharmas (*dharmātman*).
Regarding those whose remedial practices are inferior, there are the externalists with their views of permanence and annihilation.
As for the view of permanence, they reckon that the self does not perish and will receive retribution in the future.
For the sake of future retribution, one practices asceticism in the present life, which consists of eleven matters:
first, perpetual sitting, remaining seated at all times without rising;
second, the great undertaking of wandering, proceeding aimlessly through mountain valleys and dangerous terrains without stopping or avoiding them.
Third, fasting from food, which is self-starvation by abstaining from eating.
Fourth, remaining in a prostrate position, constantly standing in one place.
Fifth, following the sun by looking up at it; in the morning one looks toward the east, and as the sun rises and sets, one gazes upon it without ceasing.
Sixth, *zhì* (roasting): during the day when it is extremely hot, one uses the sun to roast the head, while setting fires on all four sides to roast the body.
Seventh, *miàn-cì* (sleeping-needles): taking needles and placing them in one spot, one sleeps upon them.
Eighth, throwing oneself from a cliff;
ninth, leaping into fire;
tenth, casting oneself into water.
Eleventh, he made offerings to the devas; he personally extracted his own sinews to serve as strings for a lute and played it as a preliminary offering to the devas.

As for those with nihilistic views (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), they maintain that when the body perishes, the self also perishes, and that there is no future or present; thus, they act according to their own whims, committing various kinds of transgressions.
This practice is not in accord with correct practice, and is therefore called "incorrect practice.

Now, observing that which is neither eternal nor annihilated—the practice of the Middle Way that avoids the two extremes—and seeing it as corresponding to the realm of Nirvāṇa, it is therefore called "correct practice."
There are two reasons why *nirvāṇa* is called a "country":
first, because it is presided over by those of great power.
These persons of great power are the Buddhas and the Pratyekabuddha Arhats; having realized *nirvāṇa*, they are free from all faults, and thus it is said that they "preside" over it.
Second, because they are not invaded by hostile thieves.
Within *nirvāṇa*, one is eternally free from afflictions (*kleśa*), which constitutes non-invasion.
Regarding the three meanings of "not planting seeds": [text follows].
First, being unwilling to go; second, taking a bypath; third, doubting the path.
If one gives rise to the view of self (*ātman*), they regard birth and death as the ultimate limit and no longer advance to seek nirvāṇa; this is the meaning of "being unwilling to go."
Though one desires to advance in pursuit, the practice of *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances) is a deviant path.
To be uncertain as to which among the eight untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative attainments and the eight tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative attainments is correct is the path of doubt.
If one cultivates untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and discriminates between right and wrong, one immediately eliminates the path of doubt.
Once the path of doubt is eliminated, the path of deviation is also eliminated.
By not clinging to birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one eliminates the refusal to depart.

Cultivating untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is able to eliminate afflictions such as the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Nirvāṇa is free from afflictions; thus, this [wisdom] is that which accords with the nature of nirvāṇa.
This matter is not erroneous; therefore, it is called "right practice.
To counteract all fears is called "renunciation.
Regarding "all fears," the Buddha asked King Prasenajit:
Some say that a great mountain comes from the east, descending across the earth and reaching up to the solar disk;
in this manner, it is clearly stated by some that great mountains likewise come from the other three directions.
"What plan do you intend to make now?
The King replied to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"

This cannot be repelled by pleasant speech, nor can it be repelled by giving, nor can it be repelled by instilling fear, nor can it be repelled by raising an army; it is not within the scope of these four expedient means.
"Just as I now must single-mindedly and urgently cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path to seek liberation.
The Buddha asked again:
"Suppose a fire were to come and scorch your head and burn your robes."
"Should you first extinguish the fire, or should you first cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path?
The King replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"The fire burns my head and my clothes; if I were to extinguish this fire, I would only temporarily escape suffering, not permanently.
If I cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path, however, I shall be forever free from suffering."
"I shall first cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path; I will not extinguish the fire first.

The mountains on the four sides are metaphors for the four sufferings of old age, illness, death, and separation from what one loves. The suffering of old age can ruin youth and vigor; the suffering of illness can rob one of strength and health; the suffering of death can topple the span of life; and the suffering of separation from what one loves can alienate one from wealth and joy.
All that has preceded consists of divergent interpretations; the positions held by Vasubandhu are identical to those of the masters of the *Upadeśa* who follow this sūtra.
The author of the treatise says:
"That which I believe and understand, I shall now set forth."
It is called impermanent because it possesses arising and ceasing.
Since conditioned phenomena possess arising and ceasing, they cannot be permanent.
Arising is existence, and ceasing is non-existence; because there is existence first and non-existence later, they are impermanent.
Why is it that arising is not a permanent arising and ceasing is not a permanent ceasing, yet one says that arising and ceasing are impermanent?
The explanation states:
because arising is destroyed by ceasing, therefore ceasing is not permanent.
Because cessation is followed by destruction and rebirth, birth is likewise impermanent.
Because its nature is contradictory [to our desires], it is called suffering.
The five aggregates are a mass of suffering; they constantly oppose the minds of sentient beings, causing them to undergo suffering.

There are no sentient beings who do not cherish the bodies they have received, nourishing them with clothing, food, drink, and various means of sustenance; yet they remain unaware of this kindness, constantly giving rise to all manner of suffering that contravenes the hearts of others. Amidst even slight increases or decreases in their food and clothing, they constantly experience distress, desiring only to attain peace and security.

Thus, when sitting for too long, suffering arises; one tires of sitting and must walk, yet walking for too long also gives rise to suffering. In this way, the four modes of deportment are constantly in conflict with one another.
The reason why it constantly contravenes the minds of sentient beings is that the objective realms upon which it depends are not real; thus, this contravention gives rise to suffering.
Because its essence is devoid [of intrinsic nature], it is called "empty."
All phenomena are merely provisional designations; they possess names and meanings, yet lack intrinsic substance.
The capacity for conditioned co-arising constitutes the meaning of "cause," and the term "cause" is established upon the basis of this conditioning.
That which is produced has the meaning of "fruit," and the name "fruit" is established with respect to that which is produced.
Yet, cause and fruit have no intrinsic nature. Why is this so?
The sense faculties and their objects combine to produce consciousness; apart from the faculties and objects, could there be any other causal entity?
Because they combine, it is said that consciousness arises; apart from this combination, could there be any further separate entity of consciousness that arises?
There is cause and effect, yet there is no agent or instrumentality; that which lacks an agent or instrumentality is what is meant by the term "having cause and effect.
Regarding "no agent": because the cause has no substantiality, there is no truly existent agent.
That which lacks functional capacity has no essence and no reality.
That which can experience suffering and pleasure has no essence within the referent of its name; this is the meaning of being "separated from essence," and is therefore called "emptiness."
Because there is no person (*pudgala*) of intrinsic nature, it is called "selfless" (*anātman*).
The Buddha taught that all existing phenomena (*dharma*) are not outside the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). If one were to say there is a self, to which of these elements would it be subsumed?
If it is not subsumed within the eighteen elements, then one knows that there is no self.
This refutes the doctrine of the Vātsīputrīya school. Their defense of their position is as follows:
"The self pervades all eighteen realms; how could it be appropriate to have it subsumed under only one distinct realm?"
The "self" they grasp is said to be neither identical nor different; it is an inexpressible treasury.

Now, we shall further refute this: for example, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and the visual object (*rūpa-viṣaya*) are the objects of perception (*ālambana*), while visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*). Consciousness arises because it takes the faculty and the object as its conditions.
Now, let us first refute [this view] regarding the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Does the self (*ātman*) that pervades the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) constitute one thing or many?

If it were different [from them], then there would necessarily be three dharmas within the object of cognition—the faculty, the object, and the self. Why, then, does the Buddha speak only of two and not of three?
If you claim that there is a self distinct from the sense faculties and their objects, yet the Buddha does not state it to be an object of cognition (*ālambana*), then this self is useless.
Furthermore, if you claim it is distinct from the sense faculties and their objects, then your assertion that it is not distinct is undermined.
If you say that the self is identical with the faculties and their objects, then there would be only the faculties and objects; where, then, would the self be?
Thus, your assertion that they are not identical is also undermined.
Next, I shall refute [the notion of a self] by means of the subjective perceiver.
Is the self identical to consciousness, or is it different?
If it were different, then there would be two types of cognizing subjects, namely the self and consciousness.
If there were two such dharmas, why did the Buddha not speak of them?
If [the self] exists but the Buddha did not teach it, then it would be useless; furthermore, your assertion that its meaning is not different from [that of consciousness] would be undermined.
